language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Abdanan County itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 61 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 46,591 people, 99.2% of the 46,977 that the atlas's own total for Abdanan County accounts for. 16 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Mojtaba Gheitasi, field notes 2016.

language.method: population-weighted sum of every published ALI settlement estimate in the unit
language.note: Nothing was read for Amlash itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 125 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2016 census population where the atlas prints one and the 2011 census population otherwise. Those weighted places hold 43,150 people, 99.8% of the 43,225 that the atlas's own total for Amlash accounts for. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Poshtvan, Hamideh, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Hamideh Poshtvan, field notes 2021.

language.method: population-weighted sum of every published ALI settlement estimate in the unit
language.note: Nothing was read for Bahar itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 71 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 123,654 people, 100.0% of the 123,654 that the settlements and towns the atlas lists in Bahar accounts for. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Izadi, Elham, Mehrdad Meshkinfam, Erik Anonby, et al. (2021), and the rows themselves cite Mehrdad Meshkinfam and Elham Izadi, field notes 2020.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Barkhar itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 42 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 108,851 people, 99.9% of the 108,933 that the atlas's own total for Barkhar accounts for. 22 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Narjes Asgari and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2020.

ethnicity.note: Iran's census does not ask ethnicity; the 2016 census asked religion in the state's recognised categories, not ethnic group.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Dalahu itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 158 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 39,215 people, 98.4% of the 39,837 that the atlas's own total for Dalahu accounts for. 13 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Fattahi, Mehdi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Mehdi Fattahi, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2017, and 100% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Ilam itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 80 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 212,671 people, 99.6% of the 213,579 that the atlas's own total for Ilam accounts for. 9 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Mojtaba Gheitasi, field notes 2016.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Kabutarahang itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 129 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 131,526 people, 100.0% of the 131,526 that the settlements and towns the atlas lists in Kabutarahang accounts for. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Izadi, Elham, Mehrdad Meshkinfam, Erik Anonby, et al. (2021), and the rows themselves cite Mehrdad Meshkinfam and Elham Izadi, field notes 2020.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Khamir itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 66 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 52,522 people, 99.2% of the 52,968 that the atlas's own total for Khamir accounts for. 7 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Mohebbi Bahmani, Hassan, Ali Rashidi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Ali Rashidi, pers. comm. 2015; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2011. The module is dated 2015, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2011-2015, and 22% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

ethnicity.note: Iran's census does not ask ethnicity; the 2016 census asked religion in the state's recognised categories, not ethnic group.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Khomeini Shahr itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 8 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 311,627 people, 100.0% of the 311,629 that the atlas's own total for Khomeini Shahr accounts for. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Saber Bakhtiari and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2020.

This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 156 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Mehran County itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 14 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 27,223 people, 99.0% of the 27,506 that the atlas's own total for Mehran County accounts for. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Gheitasi, Mojtaba, Erik Anonby, et al. (2017), and the rows themselves cite Mojtaba Gheitasi, field notes 2016.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Natanz itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 70 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 42,172 people, 99.8% of the 42,239 that the atlas's own total for Natanz accounts for. 14 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Homa Abbasi and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2018. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2018, and 100% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Parsian itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 43 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 42,837 people, 100.0% of the 42,843 that the atlas's own total for Parsian accounts for. 1 further settlement carries a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Mohebbi Bahmani, Hassan, Ali Rashidi, Erik Anonby, et al. (2015), and the rows themselves cite Ali Rashidi, pers. comm. 2015; Maryam Nourzaei, field notes 2011; Mortaza Taheri, field notes 2017. The module is dated 2015, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2011-2015, and 23% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Saqqez itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 276 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 210,747 people, 100.0% of the 210,820 that the atlas's own total for Saqqez accounts for. 6 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Mohammadirad, Masoud, Erik Anonby, et al. (2016), and the rows themselves cite Masoud Mohammadirad, field notes 2015.

ethnicity.note: Iran's census does not ask ethnicity; the 2016 census asked religion in the state's recognised categories, not ethnic group.

The data exists and is not reachable from here. Language is a different kind of gap: no Iranian census has ever asked it, so there is nothing withheld and nothing to fetch. The atlas is published province by province and has reached twelve of the thirty-one; the rest of the country is empty because those modules do not exist yet, and Kermanshah is empty because its module reaches five of its fourteen counties and under a fifth of its people.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Shahin Shahr and Meymeh itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 69 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 196,298 people, 99.9% of the 196,584 that the atlas's own total for Shahin Shahr and Meymeh accounts for. 35 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Homa Abbasi and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2018; Habib Borjian, field notes 2021. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2018-2021, and 93% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

language.method: population-weighted sum of the published ALI settlement estimates in the unit that carry a population
language.note: Nothing was read for Tiran and Karvan itself. This is the population-weighted sum of the language estimates the Atlas of the Languages of Iran publishes for 65 settlements and towns inside it, each weighted by the 2011 census population. Those weighted places hold 69,000 people, 99.9% of the 69,047 that the atlas's own total for Tiran and Karvan accounts for. 11 further settlements carry a language and no population in either census year; there is no weight to give them and none was invented, so they are excluded. ALI is a research atlas of field estimates, not a census: Iran's census does not ask language, so no census supports these shares and none contradicts them. The module is Talebi-Dastenaei, Mahnaz, Habib Borjian, Erik Anonby, et al. (2022), and the rows themselves cite Saber Bakhtiari and Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2017; Mahnaz Talebi-Dastenaei, field notes 2021. The module is dated 2022, but the fieldwork behind it is older: the rows cite field notes of 2017-2021, and 60% of the people weighted here sit behind notes taken 3 or more years before the module was published.

ethnicity.note: Iran's census does not ask ethnicity; the 2016 census asked religion in the state's recognised categories, not ethnic group.

gap_reason: The 2016 census asked religion and the Statistical Centre publishes it by province, but amar.org.ir ends the TLS handshake before a standard client can read a page (an EOF in the protocol, measured on the runner), and this project does not turn verification off. The data exists and is not reachable from here. Language is a different kind of gap: no Iranian census has ever asked it, so there is nothing withheld and nothing to fetch. Eleven provinces and 96 counties carry a figure all the same -- a population-weighted roll-up of the settlement estimates in the Atlas of the Languages of Iran, marked as the atlas's field estimates and not as anybody's count. The atlas is published province by province and has reached twelve of the thirty-one; the rest of the country is empty because those modules do not exist yet, and Kermanshah is empty because its module reaches five of its fourteen counties and under a fifth of its people.
